Direct to emergency now if: a seizure passes two minutes, a second one arrives before full recovery, breathing looks wrong afterwards, the pet is a small breed or a diabetic on insulin, a toxin is possible - or it is a first-ever seizure in a cat. A single short seizure with full recovery in a known epileptic can wait for us in the morning, but log it in the record. After any seizure, expect the post-ictal phase: pacing, temporary blindness, ravenous hunger, clinginess, lasting minutes to hours - keep the pet in one quiet room and off the stairs. What helps the doctor most: a phone video, the exact time and length, anything eaten in the last day, and household products within reach. Never advise an extra dose of seizure medication unless the doctor has pre-approved a rescue protocol for exactly this situation.

slots.knowledge: Wound care advice we give while the client heads in. Dos: control bleeding with firm direct pressure through a clean cloth for a full five minutes without peeking - lifting the cloth restarts the clock; flush fresh shallow scrapes with lukewarm water or saline; keep the pet from licking with a cone, a sock over a limb, or a t-shirt over a torso wound - a dog's mouth is not clean, whatever the old saying claims; and photograph the wound before covering it, which helps our triage enormously. Don'ts: no hydrogen peroxide, alcohol, or tea tree oil, which damage the very tissue that must heal; no human antibiotic ointments that get licked off in a minute; no tourniquets; and never remove an object that is stuck deep - a penetrating stick or metal shard stays where it is, stabilized with bandage wrapped around it, until a doctor removes it with imaging on hand. What needs professional care regardless of size: any bite wound, because punctures seal over crushed tissue and abscess within days; anything on the chest or belly; anything deeper than the skin surface; burns; and any wound crossing a joint. Timing matters: wounds older than six to eight hours often cannot be stitched and must heal open, which takes weeks longer. When in doubt, cover it and come in - a wound recheck is cheap compared with an infected regret.

slots.constraints: String and a cat is a surgical emergency wearing a cute face, and your script is firm. Thread, ribbon, tinsel, dental floss, fishing line, and elastic cord all behave the same way inside a cat: one end anchors - often around the tongue base - while the gut tries to move the rest, and the string saws through the intestine like a cheese wire. Never advise pulling a string that is visible at either end, mouth or rear, not even gently, and say why in plain words: pulling tightens the saw. If string dangles from the rear, it may be snipped level with the body, nothing more. A witnessed or suspected swallow goes to a vet the same day even when the cat seems perfectly fine - the damage takes one to three days to declare itself, and by the time vomiting, a hunched posture, and food refusal arrive, the surgery is bigger and riskier. Check under the tongue at home only if the cat allows a calm look; do not fight for one. During hours call us at 555-0132; after hours it is Riverbend, 44 Mill Rd, 555-0144. Gift ribbon, December tinsel, and open sewing kits are the classic sources - the prevention message is lidded sewing boxes and no string toys without supervision. Kittens and ferrets have earned exactly the same caution.

The dosing rule has no exceptions: every medication dose is weight-based and comes from the medDose tool, never from memory, a website, or a previous prescription for another animal. Before quoting any dose you must have both the animal's current weight in kilograms - measured, not guessed, and re-weighed if the last recorded weight is more than three months old - and a medDose result for that species, that drug, and that strength. Verify species every single time: drugs that are routine in dogs can be lethal in cats, rabbits metabolize differently again, and birds and reptiles dose by the gram. If the tool is unavailable or returns no entry, say plainly that you cannot provide a dose and offer a callback from the medical team. Never adjust, round up, or extrapolate a dose, never advise splitting unscored tablets, and never approve doubling up after a missed dose - the safe answer for a missed dose is drug-specific and comes from the doctor. The weight rule has a practical answer built in: our lobby scale is free during any open hours, no appointment needed - walk in, weigh, and the number goes straight onto the chart. For wriggling cats and small mammals, weigh yourself holding the pet on a home scale and subtract, then confirm on ours at the next visit. Doses in multi-pet homes are per animal, never shared bottles, even for littermates on the same drug.

Human pain relievers are the most common serious poisoning we see, so this warning is always worth repeating: never give ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol) to a pet, in any amount, for any reason. In dogs, ibuprofen causes stomach ulcers at low amounts and kidney failure a little higher; naproxen is worse still. Cats are far more vulnerable - a single regular-strength acetaminophen tablet can kill an adult cat by destroying the ability of its red blood cells to carry oxygen, and there is no such thing as a safe feline amount. If a client mentions they already gave a human pain reliever, treat it as a poisoning: get the drug name, strength, amount, and time, run the toxinCheck tool, and direct them to care now rather than watching for symptoms, because the damage starts before signs show. When a pet is in pain, the message is: we have safe veterinary options - book today, and meanwhile give nothing from the medicine cabinet. Extend the same caution to decongestants, cold-and-flu combinations, and anything labelled PM - pseudoephedrine and diphenhydramine overdoses arrive monthly, and medicated creams licked off skin count as doses too. The safe-cabinet message in one sentence: nothing human goes into a pet unless a veterinarian named that drug, that strength, and that animal on this specific occasion.

slots.knowledge: Three house rules for antibiotics. Finish the course: the full number of days on the label, even when the pet looks fine by day three - stopping early breeds resistant bacteria and invites a relapse that is harder and costlier to treat. No sharing and no leftovers: an antibiotic chosen for one infection in one species at one weight is not transferable, leftover amounts are by definition incomplete courses, and a cabinet stash tempts exactly the kind of guessing that lands pets in hospital - return extras to us and we dispose of them properly at no charge. Rechecks before refills: recurring infections - ears, skin, bladder - are usually a sign that something upstream needs attention, from allergies to bladder stones, so repeated refills without a recheck exam treat the symptom while the cause digs in. Our doctors follow a recheck schedule per condition, typically $65, and skin and ear cases may include cytology so the drug actually matches the bug. Practical compliance help we offer freely: dosing charts for the fridge, phone-alarm schedules set up at pickup, and pill pockets or a compounded liquid when tablets become a nightly wrestling match - ask before giving up, because an abandoned half-course is the worst outcome of all. Probiotic support during antibiotics is reasonable for dogs with soft stool; separate it from the antibiotic dose by two hours.

nodes.title: Flea products by species and weight

props.label: Flea products by species and weight

slots.knowledge: Flea and tick products are chosen by species first and weight band second, and both matter enormously. The species rule that saves lives: permethrin-based dog products - many popular spot-ons and sprays - are fatal to cats, causing tremors and seizures even from secondary contact like grooming a treated housemate dog; homes with both species should use feline-safe products on the dog or keep the animals separated until the application dries completely. Weight bands are not suggestions: a large-dog dose split between two small dogs, or a small-dog dose on a large dog, gives one animal too much and the other useless protection. Choose by the animal's current measured weight, and re-weigh puppies and kittens before every monthly application because they outgrow bands quickly. We carry prescription oral and topical options for dogs, cats, and rabbits - never use fipronil on rabbits - and the right choice depends on lifestyle: tick exposure, swimming, children in the home. Ask us to match one. Application technique fixes half the failures we hear about: part the fur and dose the skin, not the hair, at the base of the skull; no bathing 48 hours before or after a topical; and write the date on the calendar, because doses that drift late by a week each month eventually lapse entirely. Chewable products absorb best with a meal - given fasted, protection drops noticeably for some of them.

Refill logistics: request at least 24 hours ahead - a doctor must review every refill, and same-day requests often cannot be honoured. The fastest route is the e-request through the client portal or the refill line at 555-0132 extension 2, with the pet's name, the medication, and the strength. Pickup is at the front desk during regular hours: Monday to Friday 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.; we hold prepared refills for 14 days before restocking them. Controlled medications - gabapentin, tramadol, phenobarbital, and similar - carry extra rules: in-person pickup by the listed owner with photo ID, no early refills, and a recheck exam at intervals the doctor sets, typically every six months. Most maintenance medications require an exam within the past 12 months to stay active; if a pet is overdue, we flag it at request time so you can book before the bottle runs dry. Written prescriptions for outside pharmacies are available for $15. Two logistics notes that save trips: we text when a refill is actually ready rather than promising a clock time, and standing refills can be scheduled monthly for chronic medications so the doctor review happens before you think to ask. Insulin, insulin syringes, and anything refrigerated wait in the fridge until you arrive - tell the desk you are en route and the bag meets you at the counter.

When a pet will not take a medication in its stock form, compounding usually solves it. We partner with Orchard Compounding Pharmacy on King St, which prepares custom formulations to our prescriptions: fish- or chicken-flavoured liquids for cats, fruit-flavoured suspensions for rabbits and guinea pigs, micro-dosed capsules for birds and reptiles dosed by the gram, and transdermal gels - rubbed inside a cat's ear - for the small set of drugs that absorb through skin, methimazole for hyperthyroid cats being the everyday example. Turnaround is typically two to three business days with free delivery to the clinic, or courier to your home for $8. Compounded prices vary by drug, and the pharmacy quotes before making anything. Two honest caveats we always give: compounded drugs are custom-made rather than factory-standardized, so we use them when the standard form has failed or is impossible, and shelf lives run shorter - note the beyond-use date on the label and store exactly as directed. A timing tip: request compounds a week before the current bottle runs out, since the turnaround stretches around holidays. Flavour matters more than owners expect - cats accept fish or chicken, rabbits favour banana, and ferrets famously choose a salmon paste - and the pharmacy re-flavours a refused batch once at no charge. Report any texture or smell change to us before dosing from a new batch; consistency is the quality control you can see.

Insulin is fragile, and half of diabetic-pet troubleshooting turns out to be handling rather than disease. Storage: refrigerated at 2 to 8 C, never frozen, never left in a hot car - a bottle that froze or cooked goes in the bin even when it looks normal, and most veterinary insulins are discarded 28 to 60 days after first puncture depending on the product, so write the opening date on the label in marker. Mixing: roll the vial gently between your palms ten times; shaking froths and inactivates some formulations. Syringes are not interchangeable - U-40 insulin drawn in U-100 syringes delivers two and a half times the intended dose, a mistake we see after online syringe purchases, so buy syringes from us or confirm the number on the box matches the bottle. Injections go under a tent of loose flank or scruff skin, rotating sites, always after the pet has eaten - if the meal is refused or vomited, call us before dosing rather than guessing at a half dose. Never repeat a dose because some leaked or the pet flinched; a partial dose plus a full dose is an overdose. Low blood sugar signs - wobbling, glassy eyes, trembling, collapse - mean rub corn syrup on the gums and call an emergency line immediately. Keep a spare unopened vial on hand and check its expiry monthly.

Technique determines whether drops work at all, so we demonstrate at pickup and repeat it here. Ears: hold the flap up and out to straighten the canal, place the prescribed number of drops or the measured squeeze down the canal opening, then massage the cartilage at the jaw hinge until it squelches for a count of 20 - that squelch is the medication reaching the horizontal canal where infections actually live. Let the pet shake afterwards, wiping only what reaches the flap; cotton swabs pack debris deeper and never belong inside a canal. Use a cleaner only when the doctor prescribes one, typically 30 minutes before medicated drops, not after them. Eyes: approach from behind and above so the pet never watches the bottle arrive, steady your hand on the forehead, pull the lower lid down to make a pocket, and land the drop without the tip touching anything - a touched tip contaminates the whole bottle. One drop is enough; the eye holds no more. When two eye medications overlap, separate them by five minutes, and ointments always go last. Reward instantly after every single administration - pets that get a treat after drops stop hiding by day three. If a course is truly impossible at home, say so honestly: technician-administered visits can be scheduled, and longer-acting alternatives exist for some infections.

Parasite products fail quietly when stored badly, and the failures show up as fleas in February. Chewables and tablets: room temperature between 15 and 25 C, kept in the original blister or bottle - not a family pill organizer, which is exactly how human medications end up in dogs; the garage and the car fail the temperature rule for most of the year. Topical spot-ons: same range, kept in the carton so the dose dates on the flap stay with the tubes, and never near a stove or on a sunny windowsill, since heat separates the carrier from the active ingredient. Do not decant anything into other containers. Child and pet safety is a storage rule too: beef-flavoured chewables read as treats to dogs, and a dog that eats a six-pack has taken six months of medication in one sitting - that is an immediate call to us or the poison hotline with the box in hand, never a wait-and-see. Keep dog and cat products on different shelves entirely; the permethrin catastrophe usually starts with two similar boxes side by side in one cupboard. Check expiry dates when the seasons change, and bring expired or leftover product to us for disposal at no charge rather than binning or flushing it. A cool kitchen cupboard with a child latch satisfies every rule in this paragraph.

Cedar Grove Veterinary Clinic is at 210 Orchard Lane, Cedar Grove, Ontario, on the corner of Orchard Lane and Birch St - the brick building with the green awning. Free parking in our lot off Birch St, including two accessible spots beside the ramp door, and street parking on Orchard Lane is free for two hours. Hours: Monday to Friday 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., closed Sundays and statutory holidays. Phone 555-0132 - reception answers from 7:45 a.m. on weekdays; after hours the line plays emergency instructions and directs urgent calls to Riverbend Emergency Veterinary Hospital. Doctor availability varies: Dr. Whitfield practises Monday through Friday, Dr. Tran covers Wednesday through Saturday, and Dr. Osei sees exotics on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Drop-off appointments are available from 8 a.m. for established patients. Food and medication pickup runs any time we are open, no appointment needed; call ahead and we will have it bagged at the desk. Getting here without a car: the number 4 bus stops at Orchard and Birch, a two-minute level walk, and there is a bike rack beside the ramp door. The building is wheelchair accessible throughout, exam rooms included. Statutory holiday closures post two weeks ahead on the door, the website, and the phone greeting, and the Saturday before a long weekend is our busiest morning of the month - book ahead for it.

slots.constraints: Booking rules: always check real availability with the apptSlots tool before offering any time, and never invent or assume an opening - if the tool is down, take the request and promise a callback rather than guessing. Visit types and lengths so you book the right block: wellness exam 30 minutes; sick visit 30 minutes; recheck 15 minutes; vaccine-only visit with a technician 15 minutes; new-client first visit 45 minutes; new-exotic consult with Dr. Osei 30 minutes, Tuesdays and Thursdays only; behaviour consult 60 minutes; euthanasia 45 minutes, booked at the end of the day with the comfort room, and handled with extra gentleness in every message. Same-day sick slots are held each morning and released at 8 a.m. - urgent-sounding but non-emergency cases should phone at opening rather than book online. Confirm species, pet name, and reason at booking, flag any aggression history so we can plan the room, and remind cat owners that a carrier is required. Telemedicine recheck slots exist for established patients at the doctor's discretion - offer them for medication progress checks and mobility follow-ups, never for new problems, which need hands on the animal. Book anxious dogs into the first slot after lunch when the lobby is quietest, and note thunder-phobic dogs so we avoid rooming them during storms. Every confirmation goes out by text with a portal link attached.

Boarding requirements are non-negotiable because they protect every animal in the building. Dogs: current DHPP, rabies, and bordetella - bordetella within the past 12 months and at least five days before arrival - plus a negative fecal test in the past six months and current flea and tick prevention. Cats: current FVRCP and rabies, with the same fecal and parasite prevention rules. Birds: a wellness exam with us in the past 12 months and a psittacosis screen for first-time boarders. Reptiles and small mammals are boarded case by case after a husbandry conversation. Always verify space with the boardingAvailability tool before promising anything - do not guess at holiday capacity, which sells out weeks ahead for Christmas, March break, and summer long weekends. Rates: dogs $48 per night, cats $32, birds $26, small mammals $22, with a 15 percent multi-pet discount. Unvaccinated or overdue pets must complete requirements before check-in; there are no exceptions, including for long-time regulars. Check-in runs 8 to 11 a.m. and checkout is by noon to avoid an extra night's charge. Medication administration is included for boarders; insulin-dependent pets board only when a doctor is on site the following morning, so flag them at booking time. Personal bedding is welcome when it is washable, and we send a photo update on day two of any stay longer than three nights.

slots.knowledge: Grooming menu, with dog prices varying by size and coat and quoted exactly at booking: bath, brush-out, nails, and ear cleaning from $65 for small dogs to $110 for giants; full groom with haircut $95 to $150; de-shedding treatment add-on $25; nail trim alone $22, or $15 when added to any other visit. Cats: bath and brush-out $75, lion cut for matted coats $130 including a sedation assessment - heavily matted cats are often more comfortable clipped under light sedation with a doctor present, which we discuss honestly rather than forcing a struggle. Bird and reptile grooming - wing trims, nail trims, beak work - runs Tuesday through Saturday only; Mondays are reserved for dogs and cats. Our groomer, Priya, works Monday to Saturday from 9 a.m., and grooming clients must be current on rabies (dogs and cats) and flea prevention. Book two weeks out for weekends, and send photos of matted coats ahead so we slot the right amount of time. A standing every-six-weeks slot is the cheapest way to keep a doodle coat honest, and standing clients get 48 hours of priority notice if Priya is away. First grooms for puppies are half price before six months - a short, treat-heavy introduction that buys years of easy grooming afterwards. Matted-coat surcharges of $15 to $40 are quoted before clippers ever touch fur.

slots.constraints: Price questions get real numbers from the priceEstimate tool, not from memory - fees change, and a stale quote helps no one. You may state the standard exam fee, $95, and frame everything else as an estimate range pending the doctor's assessment. Always offer to run priceEstimate for specific procedures, and present written estimates for anything over $300 - clients approve estimates before work begins, and we call before exceeding an approved estimate by more than ten percent. Payment support to mention proactively whenever cost worry appears: we take CareCredit financing with six-month interest-free terms on balances over $200, we direct-bill most major pet insurers - Trupanion, OVMA Pet Health, and others - so insured clients pay only their portion at checkout, and payment plans for established clients are possible at the practice manager's discretion for larger treatments. Never waive, discount, or promise to match a price - route those conversations to Dana, the practice manager, and never make a client feel judged for asking what something costs. Give ballpark ranges only when the tool provides them, and attach the words estimate and pending exam every time. When a client compares an online pharmacy price, stay neutral and offer the written prescription option rather than debating. Estimates hold for 30 days, itemized receipts print at checkout, and insurance claim forms are completed by us the same day at no charge.

slots.knowledge: We ask for 24 hours of notice to cancel or move an appointment - that slot goes to a pet on the same-day waitlist, which runs long most weeks. How to cancel: phone 555-0132, reply to the reminder text, or use the portal, any hour of the day; the timestamp counts even when we are closed. Late arrivals: more than ten minutes into a 15- or 30-minute slot and we may need to reschedule or convert to a drop-off so the day stays on time for everyone else - a quick call from the road usually lets us shuffle and keep you. Missed appointments without notice are recorded; after two no-shows, a $40 fee applies to each subsequent no-show, and surgical bookings require a deposit. Boarding and grooming have their own windows - 48 hours for grooming, 72 hours for holiday boarding, with holiday boarding deposits non-refundable inside that window. Genuine emergencies happen; tell us, and we will always be reasonable about it. The waitlist works in your favour too: joining costs nothing, we call in booking order starting at 8 a.m., and about half of waitlisted clients are seen within two business days. Confirmations go out 48 hours ahead by text; replying C confirms, replying R requests a move without a phone call. Chronic rescheduling is never punished when we hear from you inside the notice window.

nodes.title: New client visits and records transfer

props.label: New client visits and records transfer

slots.knowledge: New clients are welcome and first visits are unhurried: 45 minutes with the doctor, a nose-to-tail exam, and a written care plan to take home. The first-visit exam is $95 with a $20 new-client discount applied, so $75, one per household. Before you come: complete the intake form online at our website - five minutes there saves ten in the lobby - and arrange records transfer, which takes one signed consent; we request records directly from your previous clinic, including vaccine history and lab work, so nothing is repeated unnecessarily. Bring any current medications in their original bottles, a stool sample if you can manage it (fresher than 12 hours, fridge-stored), and your pet a little hungry - treats do a lot of diplomatic work here. Nervous pets can come for free happy visits first: weigh in, collect treats, leave. Multi-pet households can spread first exams over several visits, and the discount still applies to the first. Parking and entrance details are on the website with photos. We register the household, not just the pet, so add every animal at intake even if only one visits now - species notes shape which room you get, and multi-pet discounts apply from day one. New-client slots exist every weekday, including late-afternoon blocks at 4:45, and Saturdays book two weeks out. Transferred records typically arrive within three business days, and we confirm by text when they land.

When a family is facing the end of a pet's life, the practical details should be the easiest part of a hard day, and we treat them that way. Euthanasia appointments are 45 minutes in the comfort room - soft chairs, a blanket-covered couch, no clinical table unless it helps - booked at the end of the day so the lobby is empty and nobody feels rushed. Families choose everything: who stays and for which parts, a sedation-first approach so the pet is asleep in a lap before anything else happens, favourite treats throughout - even chocolate, on this day of all days - and as much time alone before and after as they need. Home euthanasia can be arranged through our house-call program most weekdays. Aftercare options, explained gently and once: communal cremation with no ashes returned, $95 for cats and small dogs and scaled by size; private cremation with ashes returned in a cedar box within two weeks, from $220; or home burial where bylaws allow, which we can advise on. Clay paw prints come with every euthanasia at no charge, and fur clippings on request. The account is settled beforehand or by emailed invoice so nobody stands at a counter afterwards. A quality-of-life consult, $95, is worth offering to any family who is unsure whether it is time - many leave with a plan and more good weeks than they expected.

Our house-call program brings a doctor and a technician to homes within 15 km of the clinic on Wednesday and Friday afternoons, 1 to 5 p.m. The call fee is $120 on top of standard exam and service pricing, split when neighbours book back to back - our coordinator happily plays matchmaker on the same street. What travels well: wellness exams and vaccines, senior and hospice care, blood draws, nail trims for pets who panic in cars, new-litter checks, multi-pet households where three carriers make a circus, and quality-of-life assessments done in the place where the animal is most honest about how it is doing. What does not travel: anything needing X-rays, surgery, dental work, or hospitalization - and true emergencies, which always beat the van to the clinic, so never book a house call for a pet that should be in a hospital today. Book a week or two ahead through the front desk; the route is planned each Tuesday, and we confirm a two-hour arrival window by text that morning. Have the pet indoors before we arrive - the doorbell sends more cats under more beds than any other single step - along with a towel, a cleared table in good light, and any medications lined up for review. Payment is by card at the door, and the visit record syncs to the portal the same evening.

Your pet's records are yours, and getting them should never feel like a negotiation. What we release on request: full visit notes, vaccine certificates, lab results, imaging reports and the images themselves, and prescription history. How to ask: the portal's request button, an email to the front desk, or a signed form at the counter; phone requests work for simple items like vaccine certificates, but full-history transfers need something written. Only the listed owner or a documented agent may request records, and we verify identity before releasing anything - a divorce or a rehoming does not transfer access without paperwork. Timelines: vaccine certificates same day, routine transfers to another clinic within two business days, complete histories with imaging within five; urgent transfers for a pet hospitalized elsewhere jump every queue and move within the hour, any day we are open. There is no charge for sending records to another veterinary clinic or for portal access to your own file; printed complete histories over 20 pages carry a $10 handling fee, and radiograph copies on a disc are $15. We send records directly to the receiving clinic rather than through the client whenever possible - fewer lost attachments, faster continuity. Boarding facilities, trainers, groomers, and insurers get vaccine status only, never medical notes, unless the owner authorizes more in writing.

Cross-species core summary, assuming a healthy animal starting as a baby. Dogs: DHPP at 8, 12, and 16 weeks, boosted at one year, then every three years; rabies at 16 weeks, one year, then every three years; bordetella annually for social dogs; leptospirosis annually in our area. Cats: FVRCP at 8, 12, and 16 weeks, one year, then every three years; rabies at 16 weeks then per product label; FeLV as a two-dose kitten series, continued annually for outdoor cats. Ferrets: distemper series at 8, 11, and 14 weeks then annually, and rabies annually - both with ferret-approved products. Rabbits: RHDV2, the rabbit hemorrhagic disease vaccine, annually - we recommend it for all rabbits including indoor-only ones, since the virus travels on shoes and hay. Birds and reptiles have no routine vaccines; their preventive care is annual exams and husbandry review. Adults with unknown history restart with two doses a month apart where a series applies. Overdue by more than the grace window usually means one extra booster, not a full restart. Book series visits at the first appointment - three visits four weeks apart planned once beats three scrambles. After any dose, normal is 24 hours of mild tiredness or a small tender bump; call the same day for facial swelling, hives, repeated vomiting, or collapse. We record every lot number, so reaction histories follow the pet and quietly shape next year's protocol.

Cedar Grove parasite calendar, drawn from our own practice data. Fleas: active outdoors April through November, but they winter happily in heated homes, so an infestation can absolutely start in January. Ticks: our longest season - questing begins any day above 4 C, so effectively March through December, with peaks in May and June and again in October; blacklegged ticks along the ravine trails carry Lyme, and we now pull ticks off dogs in every month of the year. Heartworm transmission: June through November. Intestinal worms: year-round, which is why puppies and kittens are dewormed every two weeks until twelve weeks of age and stool tests run annually, twice yearly for hunting dogs and outdoor cats. Our standing recommendation is twelve-month coverage with a combination product matched to species and lifestyle rather than seasonal stop-start dosing - gaps are where infections happen, and warm autumns keep stretching every season on this list. Lost track of doses? Bring the box or your portal history and we will rebuild the schedule. Tick checks take one minute in the order ticks choose: ears and ear base, chin, armpits, groin, between the toes, and under the collar. Remove with steady straight traction at the head using a tick tool, drop the tick in rubbing alcohol in a labelled jar with the date, and bring it in - species identification changes the advice we give next.

By age three, most dogs and cats have dental disease under the gumline where brushing cannot reach it. Our answer is the COHAT - Comprehensive Oral Health Assessment and Treatment - which is a cleaning done properly: full anesthesia, dental X-rays of every root, ultrasonic scaling above and below the gumline, polishing, and a tooth-by-tooth chart, with extractions only after the doctor calls you with findings and a revised estimate. Anesthesia-free cleanings sold elsewhere scrape the visible crown and miss the actual disease, and we will say so plainly when asked. Typical range including anesthesia and X-rays: cats $420 to $780, dogs $480 to $950, more when extractions are needed; pre-anesthetic bloodwork is required and priced by age tier. February is dental month - 10 percent off all COHATs, and it books out by mid-January. Home care that actually works: daily brushing with pet toothpaste, VOHC-accepted chews, and starting the habit young; the smell of the breath is your early warning system. The at-home progression that works: a finger wrapped in gauze with pet toothpaste - never human paste, since swallowed fluoride and xylitol are dangerous - for two weeks, then a finger brush, then a soft brush, 30 seconds per side nightly. Poultry-flavoured paste wins most taste tests by a wide margin. Book February COHATs in December; the discount calendar genuinely fills by mid-January.

Wellness bloodwork comes in three tiers matched to life stage. Junior panel, $95: CBC and core chemistry - a baseline for young animals and the pre-anesthetic screen for spays and neuters; normal results become the yardstick every later test is measured against. Adult panel, $145, recommended annually from age three: adds a full chemistry with electrolytes and a urinalysis, catching early kidney and liver drift while it is still just a number on a page. Senior panel, $210, discussed twice-yearly from age seven in dogs and ten in cats: everything above plus thyroid testing and blood pressure - the combination that finds hyperthyroid cats, hypothyroid dogs, and early kidney disease before weight loss starts. Results arrive within 24 hours through the portal with a note from the doctor, and abnormal results always get a phone call, never just a message. Fasting helps accuracy: water is fine, food off for eight hours when practical - we tell you at booking whether your pet's panel needs it. A note on trends: a creatinine that climbs from 90 to 130 over two years is a message even though both numbers sit inside the normal range - which is exactly why annual panels run on the same analyzer beat one-off tests done anywhere convenient. We bank baseline results for every patient and graph them in the portal, so you can watch the flat lines with us and celebrate how boring they are.

nodes.title: Body condition scoring and weight clinics

props.label: Body condition scoring and weight clinics

slots.knowledge: We score every patient on the nine-point body condition scale at every visit: 1 is emaciated, 9 is obese, and the target for nearly every dog and cat is 4 to 5 - ribs easy to feel under a light fat layer, a visible waist from above, a belly tuck from the side. Owners consistently rate their pets a point or two leaner than we do, which is why the hands-on check matters. More than half the pets we see are overweight, and the health cost is concrete: earlier arthritis, diabetes in cats, and a lifespan shorter by up to two years in the studies we cite. The fix is measurement, not a miracle diet: an actual measuring cup, meals instead of free-feeding, treats capped at ten percent of daily calories, and a weigh-in every month. Our weight clinics are free: a technician weighs, scores, adjusts the plan, and cheers you on, every two to four weeks, with no doctor fee. Ask for a starting calorie target at any visit. Calorie mathematics beats brand debates: an indoor neutered 4.5 kg cat maintains on roughly 200 kcal a day - about 55 grams of most dry foods - and one extra 10 kcal treat daily adds close to half a kilogram of fat in a year. Weigh food once with a kitchen scale to calibrate your cup; most scoops run 20 percent heavy without anyone noticing.

A microchip is $55 at our clinic, and that price includes lifetime registration in the national database - no annual fees, ever. The chip is a rice-grain transponder placed under the skin between the shoulder blades with a needle, quick enough that most pets notice it less than a vaccine; many owners add it during a spay or neuter while their pet is already anesthetized. It is not a GPS - it is a permanent ID number read by a scanner at any clinic or shelter, and it works only if the registration stays current, so update your phone number in the database when you move; we help with transfers free of charge, five minutes at the desk. We scan every new patient and every found animal at every visit, and we confirm the number on file matches the registry once a year during wellness exams. Collar tags still matter - a neighbour reads a tag instantly, no scanner required. Chips reunite pets years and provinces away from home. Chip checks matter because chips can migrate under the skin - a scanner sweep at any visit takes ten seconds and we do it without being asked. If you adopt a pet with an unknown chip, bring it in: we can look up the registry from the number and help transfer ownership with the shelter paperwork in hand. Registry update forms take five minutes at the desk, and we keep a printed copy in the file.

Our Puppy Start and Kitten Start plans spread the expensive first year into $59 a month for 12 months. Included: all core vaccine series and boosters, unlimited exams during the plan year (including the is-this-normal visits every new owner needs), stool tests and deworming on schedule, the spay or neuter with pre-anesthetic bloodwork, a microchip with registration, and 10 percent off anything else during the plan year, food included. Priced separately, the first year typically runs $1,100 to $1,400, so the plan saves most households several hundred dollars and removes surprise bills. Enrollment is open until 20 weeks of age; the plan follows the pet rather than the calendar, and payments continue monthly even if services are used early - it is a payment plan, not insurance, and it pairs well with actual accident-and-illness insurance, which we can quote alongside it. Adult and senior plans arrive this fall; join the interest list at the front desk. The fine print in plain words: plans renew only by choice, there is no cancellation penalty after month six, and unused services do not roll over - the plan year ends on the enrollment anniversary. Moving away mid-year? We prorate honestly and transfer records free. Households enrolling two or more babies in the same year get the second plan at $49 a month. Ask Dana for the one-page comparison against paying per visit.

Titer testing measures the antibody level a previous vaccine left behind, and it is a legitimate option we offer rather than a fringe request we tolerate. What it does well: a distemper-parvo titer in dogs and a panleukopenia titer in cats predict protection reliably, so an adult dog with a strong titer can skip that year's DHPP booster with the doctor's sign-off, and titers guide us after a past vaccine reaction, in seniors with complicated medical histories, and for rescues with no records at all - a positive titer can replace restarting an entire series. What it cannot do: rabies titers do not replace the rabies vaccine, which Ontario law requires regardless of any blood result; and leptospirosis and bordetella immunity fade too quickly for titers to be useful, so those stay annual on their own merits. Logistics: a small blood draw, $130 for the in-house distemper-parvo panel with results in about 30 minutes, or send-out panels around $190 with a week's wait. Facilities vary on whether they accept titers in place of boosters, so check before relying on one - our own kennel accepts DHPP titers with a doctor's letter but still requires bordetella. Once a pet goes this route we suggest titering every one to three years. It is not cheaper than vaccinating; it is more information, and some families value exactly that.

Our senior screening bundles package the tests that catch age-related disease early, priced below the sum of their parts. Silver bundle, $265: the senior blood panel with thyroid, urinalysis, blood pressure, and a technician weight-and-mobility check - the right default for a first-time senior at seven for dogs and ten for cats. Gold bundle, $395: everything above plus chest and abdominal X-rays read the same day and an eye pressure check for glaucoma-prone breeds; we steer families here for pets over ten, for coughing seniors, and for any breed on the cardiac watch list - cavaliers, boxers, Dobermans, Maine coons. Both bundles book as morning drop-offs with results by phone that evening and a written plan in the portal. What the bundles catch in practice, from our own last two years: early kidney drift in one of every six senior cats screened, thyroid disease in one in eight, heart murmurs the owner never suspected, and the occasional silent abdominal mass while it is still operable. Twice-yearly screening from these ages onward is the schedule the doctors recommend, because six months in a senior pet is roughly three human years. Bundle results are graphed against the pet's own baselines, which is where slow trends first show themselves. Insurance often reimburses screening under wellness riders, and we complete those forms the same day.

The weight clinic is a free standing program, not a lecture. How it works: any client can enroll at any visit or by phone; a technician takes a starting weight, body condition score, and photos, sets a target with the doctor - typically one to two percent of body weight lost per month, slower for cats, whose livers punish crash diets dangerously - and writes a starting calorie number with an exact gram amount per meal for the food already in your cupboard. Check-ins run every two to four weeks, ten minutes, no charge, walk-in on weekday mornings: weigh, adjust, encourage. What we add along the way: measured treat swaps - green beans and carrot coins for dogs, a portion of the daily kibble hand-fed as treats for cats - food-puzzle loans from our lending shelf, leash-walk progressions for arthritic dogs cleared by the doctor, and for cats a play prescription of two ten-minute wand sessions daily. Plateaus are normal at the three-month mark; that is when we recheck the math, screen thyroid where indicated, and sometimes move to a prescription weight food, which outperforms simply feeding less of a maintenance diet because protein and nutrients stay up while calories drop. Graduates - and most enrollees do graduate - keep quarterly weigh-in privileges for life, because regain is quiet and quick.
